title: Changing a Habit
objective: After this level you can apply cues, rewards and if-then plans to change a real habit.
summary: Habits run in stable settings, so changes of context and if-then plans that tie a new routine to a cue help change them; rewards keep the new routine going.

cards.headline: Much of what you do today, you did yesterday, in the same place.
cards.body: In 2002 diary studies led by Wendy Wood, students wrote down what they were doing each time a watch chimed. Between a third and a half of their behaviors were done almost daily in the same place, often while they thought about something else. If so much runs on autopilot, how do you change a habit?

cards.headline: Habits live in places
cards.body: Wood's finding points to the lever: habits tend to repeat in the same setting. Disrupt the setting and a habit loosens. In a 2016 field experiment in Peterborough, England, by Bas Verplanken and Deborah Roy, a push toward greener habits worked better on people who had moved house within about three months. A move scrambles the old cues and opens a window.

cards.headline: Write an if-then plan
cards.body: Wanting a change isn't enough; a goal alone doesn't guarantee action. An implementation intention, or if-then plan, spells out when, where and how you'll act: "If situation Y happens, then I'll do X." For example: "If I pour my morning coffee, then I'll put on my walking shoes." The plan borrows a cue that already exists and hangs the new routine on it.

cards.fact: Across 94 tests, if-then plans had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
cards.context: In 2006, Peter Gollwitzer and Paschal Sheeran pooled 94 tests with more than 8,000 people. If-then plans helped people get started and shield their goals from unwanted distractions. Then let the new routine pay off: as B. F. Skinner argued, consequences such as reinforcement are major drivers of behavior.

When, where and how you will act

options.rationale: The plan links a situation to an action.

questions.prompt: Ana wants to floss every night but keeps forgetting. Which plan best uses this level's research?

options.label: "I really will try harder to floss."
options.rationale: A goal alone doesn't guarantee action.

options.label: "I'll floss whenever I happen to remember."
"I'll floss once I feel more motivated."
options.rationale: That waits on a feeling instead of a cue.

options.label: "If I finish brushing my teeth, then I'll floss."

questions.explanation: Tying flossing to an existing cue in an if-then plan spells out when, where and how, which helps people act.
